Aparna: Made ten Diwali cards last night! Marigolds and little diyas 🙂
Lalremsiami: Only ten? Why not fifty?
Aparna: Paper and paint cost money. If nobody buys, I'm stuck with forty. Ten first.
Lalremsiami: Fair. Who's buying?
Aparna: Relatives, neighbours, Sir at tuition. I'll carry them in a folder.
(two days later)
Aparna: Sold eight! Two aunts, three neighbours, Sir bought one for his mother.
Lalremsiami: Nice!! So make more?
Aparna: Two cousins asked for Bhai Dooj ones. Nobody wanted the star ones. So twenty-five more, only diya and Bhai Dooj designs.
Lalremsiami: Smart. Save me one 😊

qa.q: How many cards did Aparna sell in two days?
What might Aparna be feeling about the sales?
qa.a: Encouraged and cautiously excited: eight cards sold, and the plan for more is based on which designs people actually asked for.

qa.q: What else could Aparna do to learn from buyers, and why?
qa.a: Ask each buyer which card they liked best and what they would pay, because direct answers cost nothing and guide the next batch.

qa.q: How might a neighbour who bought a card see Aparna's plan?
qa.a: A neighbour gets an affordable handmade gift and the pleasure of supporting a local student, and their choice of design helps Aparna decide what to make.

grounding: A student makes ten cards, sells them to relatives and neighbours and uses the response to decide about making more.

passage:
In Kalwa town, Sudha wanted to start a small business before Diwali. Her friend Rajni suggested a stall in the market. Sudha shook her head. "What if nobody buys anything? I'd waste all my savings."

Instead, she bought one sheet of coloured card, glue and some glitter, and made ten greeting cards at the kitchen table with little hand-painted diyas. Her mother gave her an old shoebox to keep them in.

That weekend she took the box to her aunt's house, then to three neighbours. She sold eight in two days. One neighbour asked, "Can you write 'Happy Diwali' in Marathi too?" Another said the glitter came off on her hands.

Sudha wrote down every comment. Then she made twenty more: some in Marathi, no loose glitter. This time Rajni helped her sell at the temple gate. They sold eighteen.

qa.q: How many cards did Sudha make at first?
What was Sudha worried about when she refused the market stall?
qa.a: She was anxious that nobody would buy anything and she would lose her savings.

qa.q: What could Sudha do next, based on the second batch?
qa.a: She could ask buyers what else they would like, such as wedding or birthday cards, before making a larger batch.

qa.q: How might the neighbour who asked for Marathi cards feel about the new batch?
qa.a: That neighbour would probably feel pleased and listened to, seeing the suggestion turned into new cards.

grounding: Shows a student making ten handmade greeting cards for the festival season, selling to relatives and neighbours and using the response to decide on making more.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version of a small business [Action]
passage:
In Enugu, three weeks before Christmas, Chidi had an idea: selling handmade decorations. His older cousin Leila, who ran a hair salon, said, "Start small. Don't buy a whole market stall of materials."

So Chidi made just ten star ornaments from painted bottle caps and wire, working on the veranda after school. He took them to church on Sunday and to his aunties' houses.

He sold seven. An auntie said the wire hook was too sharp for small children's hands. A neighbour asked if he could paint names on them. A man at church said they were too small to see on a tree.

Chidi went back to the veranda with a notebook. Bigger caps. Bent-over hooks. Names painted to order. He made fifteen more.

Leila let him display them on her salon counter. By Christmas Eve, he'd sold all fifteen and had six name orders waiting.

qa.q: How many star ornaments did Chidi make first?
How might Chidi have felt reading the comments in his notebook?
qa.a: He probably felt encouraged and curious, seeing the comments as ways to improve rather than as rejection.

qa.q: What else could Chidi try after Christmas?
qa.a: He could try a small batch for another occasion, like birthdays, and again learn from the first buyers before making more.

qa.q: How does Chidi's approach look to Leila?
qa.a: Leila seems supportive and pleased, since her advice to start small worked and she offered her salon counter.

grounding: Shows a teen making ten handmade decorations for the festive season, selling to relatives and neighbours and using the feedback to decide how many more to make.
